meta.title: Train, Validation, and Test Splits
meta.thesis: Train, Validation, and Test Splits is practical when learners can apply it to this concrete case: A subscription churn model needs splits that predict future users rather than memorize the past. By the end, they should be able to build or review time-aware split plan with train, validation, and final test partitions, measure test result remains stable after launch, and catch the failure where random splitting leaks near-duplicate users across partitions.

mentalMap.title: Train, Validation, and Test Splits: mental map
mentalMap.caption: Create honest evaluation by splitting before training, using train for fitting, validation for choices, test for final estimate, and leakage-aware split strategies.
mentalMap.oneLineThesis: Clean train, validation, and test splits are the foundation of trustworthy model evaluation.

modules.title: Split before learning to get an honest exam
modules.sub: Evaluation starts before the first model fit.
modules.summary: A split creates examples the model cannot learn from directly.
objectives: Explain why data is split before training.
Map train, validation, and test to roles.
Anchor the lesson in ticket-priority classification.

blocks.title: The model should not see the exam while studying

spans.text: Problem anchor: a team builds a ticket-priority classifier. If the same customer issue, duplicate ticket, or future pattern appears in both training and evaluation, the score can look excellent while the deployed model fails. Splitting is how we create an honest exam.
Train data fits model parameters. Validation data helps choose features, thresholds, and hyperparameters. Test data estimates final performance after choices are made.

blocks.analogy: Train is practice, validation is rehearsal feedback, and test is opening night.

spans.text: Start with 1000 labeled tickets. Before fitting text vectorizers or models, assign 700 to train, 150 to validation, and 150 to test. If multiple tickets come from the same customer incident, keep the incident in one split so the model cannot memorize the duplicate wording.

blocks.title: Split timing
blocks.prompt: When should you split the dataset?

options.text: After choosing the best model from all rows.
Before fitting features, models, thresholds, or preprocessing learned from the data.
Only after deployment.

blocks.explanation: Splitting early protects the evaluation promise.

modules.title: Train fits parameters, validation chooses decisions
modules.summary: Training learns weights; validation guides model selection.
objectives: Describe what training data is allowed to do.
Use validation for hyperparameters and thresholds.

spans.text: Training data is used for fitting parameters: weights, tree splits, centroids, or learned preprocessing. Validation data is used to choose decisions: model family, regularization strength, threshold, features, or prompt/reranker setting. The test set waits until those choices are locked.

The ticket classifier outputs risk scores. On validation, threshold 0.70 catches most urgent tickets but creates many false alarms; threshold 0.85 misses too many urgent cases. The team chooses 0.76 from validation because it matches support capacity. They do not keep adjusting after looking at test.

modules.title: Test estimates final generalization once
modules.sub: The test set answers one question after choices are locked.
modules.summary: A clean test set gives a less biased final performance estimate.
objectives: Document the model-selection freeze before test.

blocks.title: The test set loses power each time you peek

spans.text: A test set is useful because the model-selection process has not adapted to it. If you test, tweak, test, tweak, the test set becomes part of the design loop. The reported score becomes too optimistic.

modules.title: Leakage breaks the promise
modules.sub: Information can leak through features, preprocessing, duplicates, or time.
modules.summary: Leakage makes evaluation look better than deployment reality.
objectives: Run a simple split leak checker.
Verify AI-generated pipelines fit preprocessing on train only.

blocks.title: Leak check for grouped ticket splits

spans.text: This tiny check catches a grouped leakage problem: customer A appears in train and test, so the evaluation may reward memorized customer-specific language.

predictThenReveal.prompt: Predict the printed overlap. Which split pair leaks?
predictThenReveal.answer: It prints train_test with customer A. The model could learn customer-specific patterns from train and look artificially good on test.

spans.text: Checklist: split before fitting vectorizers/scalers/encoders; fit preprocessing on train only; transform validation and test with train-fitted preprocessing; group duplicates together; use time-based split for future prediction; and never tune on test.

modules.title: Stratified, grouped, and time splits match the data story
modules.sub: The right split depends on labels, related records, and time.
modules.summary: Split strategy should reflect what deployment will ask the model to do.
objectives: Choose random, stratified, grouped, or time-based splits.
Explain why rare labels need stratification.

blocks.title: There is no universal honest split

spans.text: Random splits can work when rows are independent and label balance is healthy. Stratified splits preserve rare label proportions. Grouped splits keep related records, such as one customer or patient, together. Time-based splits evaluate whether the model trained on the past works on the future.

blocks.ruleOfThumb: Choose the split that mimics the deployment question.
blocks.useWhen: Use stratified splits for rare labels, grouped splits for related entities, and time splits for forecasting or changing processes.
blocks.avoidWhen: Avoid random splits when duplicates, users, sessions, documents, or future information can cross the boundary.

blocks.title: Split choice
blocks.prompt: A fraud model predicts future transactions and patterns drift monthly. Which split is most appropriate?

options.text: A random split that mixes future and past freely.
A time-based split that trains on earlier transactions and evaluates later ones.
A split after scaling on all rows.

blocks.explanation: The split should match the deployment timeline.

ai.label: AI
ai.laymanDefinition: Software systems that perform tasks associated with human intelligence.
ai.technicalNote: In these foundations lessons, AI is the broad field; the concrete mechanisms are models, data, objectives, and evaluation loops.

ml.label: ML
ml.laymanDefinition: A branch of AI where systems learn patterns from data instead of only following hand-written rules.
ml.technicalNote: ML work is defined by training data, features, models, objectives, validation, and deployment constraints.

model.label: Model
model.laymanDefinition: A learned or configured function that maps inputs to predictions, scores, clusters, or generated outputs.
model.technicalNote: Model choice encodes assumptions such as linearity, distance, tree splits, capacity, or sequential reward.

loss.label: Loss
loss.laymanDefinition: A numerical training signal that measures how wrong a prediction is for a task.
loss.technicalNote: Loss drives optimization; it is not the same as product quality, fairness, or final generalization.

generalization.label: Generalization
generalization.laymanDefinition: The ability of a model to perform well on examples it did not train on.
generalization.technicalNote: Generalization is checked with validation/test data, leakage audits, and slice monitoring.

pipeline.label: Pipeline
pipeline.laymanDefinition: A repeatable sequence of data transforms, feature steps, model fitting, and evaluation or inference.
pipeline.technicalNote: Pipelines prevent train/test leakage and keep preprocessing identical between training and production.

capstone.prompt: Design splits for a ticket-priority classifier. Decide whether to split randomly, by customer, or by time; write which preprocessing fits only on train; define validation decisions; and reserve test for one final estimate. Next rung: add cross-validation or grouped CV.
checks: Validation choices are not made on test data.

finalCheck.title: Knowledge check
finalCheck.intro: A quick check across the whole lesson — pick or type your answers.

questions.prompt: You build a ticket-priority classifier and want an honest estimate of how it will perform on brand-new support tickets your team has never seen. Which split gives you that honest estimate?

options.text: Training set — it has the most data, so the accuracy will be most reliable.
Validation set — you already used it to tune the model, so you know it works.
Test set — it is held out completely until after all decisions are made.
Any split works as long as you shuffle the data first.

questions.explanation: The test set is kept untouched until the very end, so its accuracy reflects true generalization — not memorization of data the model or developer has already seen.

questions.prompt: During development you try five different decision thresholds for flagging a ticket as 'urgent' and pick the one with the best F1 score. Which dataset should you use for this comparison?

options.text: Test set, because F1 is a final metric.
Validation set, because choosing thresholds is a tuning decision.
Training set, because it has the most examples to score against.
A brand-new dataset collected after deployment.

questions.explanation: Threshold selection is a hyperparameter decision; using the validation set for it keeps the test set clean and unbiased.

questions.prompt: A teammate fits a TF-IDF vectorizer on the entire dataset (train + validation + test combined) before splitting. What problem does this cause, and what should they do instead?
questions.acceptableAnswer: This is data leakage: the vectorizer has seen vocabulary and word frequencies from the test set, so test-set evaluation is no longer honest. The fix is to fit the vectorizer only on the training data, then use transform (not fit_transform) on the validation and test sets.
questions.explanation: Fitting any preprocessor on data that includes the test set leaks information into the model pipeline, making test performance look better than it really is.

questions.prompt: Your ticket dataset has 90 % 'low-priority' tickets and only 10 % 'urgent' tickets. You do a plain random 80/20 split. What is the main risk?

options.text: The split will take too long to compute on large datasets.
The validation or test fold may end up with very few 'urgent' examples, making evaluation unreliable.
Random splits always leak data between folds.
The training set will contain too many duplicate tickets.

questions.explanation: With rare labels, random splits can produce folds where the minority class is severely under-represented; stratified splitting preserves the class ratio in every fold.

questions.prompt: After weeks of tuning you check the test set, see a lower score than expected, and adjust one more hyperparameter to improve it. Why is this a problem?

options.text: It isn't a problem — using the test set for one final adjustment is standard practice.
It wastes compute because the model was already good enough.
The test set is now effectively a second validation set, so reported accuracy is optimistic and no longer an honest estimate.
Hyperparameters can only be changed before any data is collected.

questions.explanation: Every time you make a decision based on test-set feedback, you overfit to that set; the reported score then flatters the model and cannot be trusted as a real-world estimate.
